newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Urine-throwing fans menace Central American soccer.
newsitem.headline: Urine-throwing fans menace Central American soccer.

text.p: Brawling, urine-throwing fans in crowded stands make soccer stadiums throughout Central America disasters waiting to happen, as in Guatemala, where up to 82 fans were crushed to death before a game last week.

In a region once known for its violent political conflicts, soccer matches have long been another social battleground. The poor, on high-level terraces, hurl objects at the rich in plush seats below, at referees, at the enemy team and at each other.
One of the weapons of choice -- urine -- is hurled in cups. In El Salvador, which borders Guatemala, conflict is so savage that the standing-only areas are known locally as "Vietnam."
The potential danger has never been a secret.
"Some sectors get aggressive because of all the alcohol they have imbibed. Guatemalans have always known that it is risking life or limb to go to a big game," said local sports writer Felix Mencos.
Guatemala's worst sporting disaster happened last Wednesday night, when fans were crushed to death just before a World Cup qualifying game in hopelessly overcrowded Mateo Flores stadium.
The government says unruly crowds may have been one of the factors, alleging that a brawl on the terraces triggered a human avalanche down the stands, smothering those below.
From Britain to Argentina, boisterous, beer-drinking soccer fans are famous for violence and mayhem.
But Central America has its own particular brand of soccer hooliganism and bizarre stadium rituals, played out week after week on the general admission cement terraces with no individual seats.
In El Salvador, Costa Rica and Guatemala, men routinely urinate into cups or bags and throw the product onto the field or onto other fans below.
Necessity may be the mother of the urine ritual. No aisles divide the terraces so once fans are lodged at the top they are stuck there with no bathroom breaks for beer guzzlers.

In Costa Rica fans have brought buckets of rocks to national championship games. President Jose Maria Figueres, who witnessed the aftermath of the Guatemalan tragedy has called for a review of stadium security in his country.
In El Salvador, any couple entering a soccer match can expect to run a gauntlet along the bottom of the stands as men belt them with bags of water.

Most stadiums in the region do not have crowd control barriers to manage the flow of people in and out of entrances. Huge bottlenecks form and some peoples' feet are swept off the ground as the multitude surges toward the entrances.

In many soccer stadiums in Central America large chainlink fences ring the playing fields. When the stands fill up, fans are pressed six deep against the wire, sometimes unable to move during an entire game.

Many ordinary Guatemalans and the press said fans with forged tickets were the main cause of the overcrowding last week but they also acknowledged supporters were at a fever pitch of excitement before the match against Costa Rica.
"Our problem is we are fanatics, not fans," said Marco Antonoio Alfaro, who was mourning five members of one family who died at Guatemala's national stadium.
"The people don't have any manners and even less fear of God," said Lionel Ardon Rodriguez, another mourner attending the burial of a 13-year-old relative on Friday.

After analysing the Guatemalan tragedy, FIFA, world soccer's governing body, asked France, which will host the World Cup finals in 1998, to pull down perimeter fences at its venues. Major safety improvements in Central American stadiums, though, are less likely.
